newsitem.title: USA: U.S. concerned about South Korean missiles.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concerned about South Korean missiles.

text.p: U.S. officials acknowledged concerns on Tuesday about South Korea's missile programme but said talks this week made progress in resolving differences.
"I think that as a result of these talks some of our concerns have been allayed. Did we have concerns going in? Yes," a senior U.S. official told reporters.
The talks took place on Monday and Tuesday in Washington between U.S. and South Korean officials who comprise a bilateral task force on non-proliferation.

The Washington Times reported Monday that South Korea -- a key U.S. ally in Asia -- was building a long-range cruise missile that violates a 1979 U.S.-South Korean agreement restricting Seoul from developing missiles with ranges greater than 112 miles (180.2 km).

It said the missile programme is a sign that South Korea is moving ahead with plans to counter the threat posed by North Korea's missiles, including the 620-mile- (997.8-km-) range No Dong missile that was set for flight testing several weeks ago.

The talks were expected to focus on Seoul's request to alter the 1979 agreement to permit South Korea to build missiles with ranges up to 186 miles (299.3 km) -- the range allowed under the 31-nation Missle Technology Control Regime (MTCR), the newspaper reported.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the talks "centered on issues of common concern -- both bilateral and multilateral."

These involved "missile proliferation and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, our shared objective with the government of South Korea about its future membership in the Missile Technology Control Regime -- we want to see South Korea become a member of that organisation -- and the importance of working with South Korea and others in implementing the Chemical Weapons Convention," he said.
The two sides also discussed further cooperation in support of their mutual non-proliferation objectives, both in Asia and around the world, said Burns.
He termed the talks "very successful ... They made some progress."
Burns refused to say if the United States believed that South Korea was complying with the 1979 agreement, which officials said had been confidential up to this point.

But he hinted at some violation, telling reporters: "As South Korea looks to the future, of course, we want to make sure that it is a member of the MTCR, is in compliance with its commitments, and we have every reason to believe that will be the case."
Officials said privately that South Korea is concerned about missile development in Stalinist North Korea, its arch rival, "and this is what they talked to us about."
South Korea reportedly wants to replace the 1979 agreement with membership in the MTCR, thus allowing Seoul to obtain longer-range missile technoolgy and equipment from other MTCR members.
